newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Spain said on track to fulfil EMU criteria.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Spain said on track to fulfil EMU criteria.

text.p: Growth is going up, inflation is going down and Spain is now mature enough to join the launch of Europe's common currency, the Economy Ministry's independent economic advisors said on Wednesday.
Data for 1997 will determine which nations help found the euro currency in two years. The numbers for Spain, once Europe's economic ugly duckling, are looking better all the time.

The experts, known as the wise men, revised their forecast for 1997 gross domestic product (GDP) growth to 3.2 percent from the 2.9 percent they had foreseen in January. In 1998, growth will accelerate to 3.5 percent, they say.
And despite the economic revival, inflation is now forecast to end the year at a modest 1.8 percent, much more moderate than the 2.6 percent they had foreseen in January.
The numbers add up to good news for Spain's European ambitions, once seen as an impossible dream.
"Spain will fulfil, without difficulty, all the convergence criteria and will be able to join the common currency from the start," the wise men said in a statement.

Of the five economic requirements, Spain has already managed to stabilise its once devaluation-prone currency for two years and bring down bloated long-term interest rates to within a short distance of its more stable northern neighbours.
Inflation has moderated to less than half the rate it was at just six months ago and the public deficit is on track to narrow to three percent of GDP.
In short, Spain will meet inflation and budget criteria for joining a single euro currency without breaking into a sweat, the experts said.
The fifth criterion, which requires public debt of less than 60 percent of GDP, would not be met but the percentage would fall, allowing Spain to join.
But despite progress towards EMU criteria, key money rates are unlikely to fall much further, after a four percentage point decline to 5.25 percent in just a year and a half, they said.

Still, Spain has managed an economic overhaul that was considered unrealistic just over a year ago and has continued to show improvement while other, core members of the European currency project have stumbled.
"Spain is now one of the countries with the best results in terms of convergence among candidates for the euro," they added.
The domestic advisors are not alone in praising Spain's progress.

In April, the EU Commission forecast that Spain's conservative government would meet its deficit goals. And in June, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development gave it top marks for its progress.
Spain's one-year-old conservative government made joining the euro at its launch the cornerstone of its European policy in an attempt to shed the nation's isolationist past.
And the advisors applauded the effort.
"Every nation will come out a winner (from the euro). But Spain will benefit in particular - we're already benefiting in advance," advisor Angel Laborda told a news conference.
